manifest.title: NP-Hardness of (3,4)-SAT and [2,3]-Bounded 3-SAT

inputs.abstract:
*(3,4)-SAT* is satisfiability restricted to formulas in which every clause has exactly three
literals and every variable occurs at most four times. Tovey (1984, Theorem 2.3) proved that
it is NP-hard. This submission proves that theorem: every language in NP has a
polynomial-time many-one reduction to (3,4)-SAT, on the CNF encoding and the Turing
machines of the archive's Cook–Levin theorem.

The reduction starts from unrestricted satisfiability. Every literal occurrence gets a fresh
variable, and a cycle of implications forces the copies of one variable to take the same
value. Each clause is then broken up through link variables into a chain of clauses of at
most three literals. Finally every clause with fewer than three literals is filled up with
the negation of a fresh variable, which a private copy of Tovey's thirteen-clause gadget
forces to be true.

Following the archive's convention for reductions, the concepts state the construction as
definitions, then its correctness, then its running time. The reduction is proved correct
and proved to run in polynomial time: it is a program for the archive's word RAM, and
polynomial time on the word RAM transfers to Turing machines.

The submission also proves the variant that the scheduling reductions start from,
*[2,3]-bounded 3-SAT*: every clause has two or three literals and every literal occurs at
most twice. It is NP-hard on the self-delimiting binary encoding of formulas that the
scheduling submissions read. The reduction is from (3,4)-SAT. Every literal position of the
formula gets its own variable, so no variable occurs more than once among the clauses of
three literals, and the copies of an original variable are tied together by a cycle of
two-literal implications, in which every copy occurs once positively and once negatively.
This second step is proved correct on formulas whose clauses all have three literals, which
is what the first reduction produces, and its word RAM program is proved to run in
polynomial time. Neither reduction has a parameter, so there is no parameter bound to prove.

concepts.title: The Reduction from Satisfiability to (3,4)-Satisfiability
concepts.description:
A CNF formula $F$ with $N$ literal occurrences, over variables below $V$, is turned into a
(3,4) formula in two steps.

*Splitting.* The occurrence at position $p$ of a variable $v$ is replaced by a fresh
variable $w_{v,p}$. A clause is chained through link variables $z_p$: the clause
$(l_0 \vee \dots \vee l_{L-1})$ becomes
$(l_0 \vee z_0), (\bar z_0 \vee l_1 \vee z_1), \dots, (\bar z_{L-2} \vee l_{L-1})$, and an
empty clause stays empty. For every $v$, the implications $w_{v,p+1} \to w_{v,p}$, taken
cyclically over all positions, force the copies of $v$ to agree. Afterwards every clause
has at most three literals and every variable occurs at most three times.

*Padding.* Each clause with fewer than three literals is filled up with literals $\bar y$,
where every $y$ is a fresh variable that a private copy of Tovey's gadget forces to be
true. The gadget has thirteen clauses on ten variables: $y$ occurs three times in it and
each of the other nine variables four times.

On words, the reduction decodes a formula, applies the two steps and encodes the result. A
word that encodes no formula is treated as the formula consisting of one empty clause.

sections.title: Formalization Notes
sections.markdown:
The copies $w_{v,p}$ are created and tied together for all $v < V$ and $p < N$, not only
for the pairs $(v, p)$ that occur. This way the cyclic successor of a position is simply
the next position, at the price of an output of quadratic size.

import Lax345332.ThreeFourSat

/-!
---
title: The Reduction from Satisfiability to (3,4)-Satisfiability
type: definition
---
A CNF formula $F$ with $N$ literal occurrences, over variables below $V$, is turned into a
(3,4) formula in two steps.

*Splitting.* The occurrence at position $p$ of a variable $v$ is replaced by a fresh
variable $w_{v,p}$. A clause is chained through link variables $z_p$: the clause
$(l_0 \vee \dots \vee l_{L-1})$ becomes
$(l_0 \vee z_0), (\bar z_0 \vee l_1 \vee z_1), \dots, (\bar z_{L-2} \vee l_{L-1})$, and an
empty clause stays empty. For every $v$, the implications $w_{v,p+1} \to w_{v,p}$, taken
cyclically over all positions, force the copies of $v$ to agree. Afterwards every clause
has at most three literals and every variable occurs at most three times.

*Padding.* Each clause with fewer than three literals is filled up with literals $\bar y$,
where every $y$ is a fresh variable that a private copy of Tovey's gadget forces to be
true. The gadget has thirteen clauses on ten variables: $y$ occurs three times in it and
each of the other nine variables four times.

On words, the reduction decodes a formula, applies the two steps and encodes the result. A
word that encodes no formula is treated as the formula consisting of one empty clause.

# Formalization Notes

The copies $w_{v,p}$ are created and tied together for all $v < V$ and $p < N$, not only
for the pairs $(v, p)$ that occur. This way the cyclic successor of a position is simply
the next position, at the price of an output of quadratic size.
-/

namespace Lax345332.Construction

open Lax429075.CNF Lax429075.Encoding Lax434930.PolynomialTime Lax345332.ThreeFourSat

-- The gadget

/-- Tovey's thirteen clauses on the variables `g, g+1, …, g+9`; they force `g` to be true. -/
def gadget (g : ℕ) : Formula :=
  let y := g
  let a (j : ℕ) := g + 1 + 3 * j
  let b (j : ℕ) := g + 2 + 3 * j
  let d (j : ℕ) := g + 3 + 3 * j
  ((List.range 3).map fun j => [⟨y, true⟩, ⟨a j, true⟩, ⟨b j, true⟩]) ++
  ((List.range 3).flatMap fun j =>
    [[⟨d j, true⟩, ⟨a j, true⟩, ⟨b j, false⟩], [⟨d j, true⟩, ⟨a j, false⟩, ⟨b j, true⟩],
     [⟨d j, true⟩, ⟨a j, false⟩, ⟨b j, false⟩]]) ++
  [[⟨d 0, false⟩, ⟨d 1, false⟩, ⟨d 2, false⟩]]

-- Padding

/-- The base of the `t`-th gadget of the `k`-th clause, above the variables below `B`. -/
def ybase (B k t : ℕ) : ℕ := B + 30 * k + 10 * t

/-- The padding literals of a clause of length `n`. -/
def pads (B k n : ℕ) : Clause := (List.range (3 - n)).map fun t => ⟨ybase B k t, false⟩

/-- The `k`-th clause, padded, with its three gadgets. -/
def unit (B k : ℕ) (C : Clause) : Formula :=
  (C ++ pads B k C.length) ::
    (gadget (ybase B k 0) ++ gadget (ybase B k 1) ++ gadget (ybase B k 2))

/-- Every clause of `G`, padded to three literals and followed by its gadgets. `B` bounds the
variables in use. -/
def pad (B : ℕ) (G : Formula) : Formula :=
  (List.range G.length).flatMap fun k => unit B k (G.getD k [])

-- Splitting

/-- The copy of the variable `v` at position `p`. -/
def wv (V v p : ℕ) : ℕ := v + p * V

/-- The link variable after position `p`. -/
def zv (V N p : ℕ) : ℕ := V * N + p

/-- A placeholder literal, used when an index is past the end of a list. -/
def dflt : Literal := ⟨0, false⟩

/-- The `i`-th clause of the chain of `C`, whose first literal sits at position `o`: the
negated link before it (except for `i = 0`), the copy of the `i`-th literal, and the link
after it (except for the last). -/
def chainClause (V N o : ℕ) (C : Clause) (i : ℕ) : Clause :=
  (if i = 0 then [] else [⟨zv V N (o + i - 1), false⟩]) ++
    [⟨wv V (C.getD i dflt).index (o + i), (C.getD i dflt).positive⟩] ++
    (if i + 1 = C.length then [] else [⟨zv V N (o + i), true⟩])

/-- The chain of the clause `C`, whose first literal sits at position `o`; an empty clause
becomes one empty clause. -/
def chainClauses (V N o : ℕ) (C : Clause) : Formula :=
  if C.length = 0 then [[]] else (List.range C.length).map (chainClause V N o C)

/-- The chains of all clauses of a formula, the first literal of the formula being at
position `o`. -/
def chains (V N : ℕ) : ℕ → Formula → Formula
  | _, [] => []
  | o, C :: F => chainClauses V N o C ++ chains V N (o + C.length) F

/-- The cyclic successor on positions. -/
def next (N p : ℕ) : ℕ := if p + 1 < N then p + 1 else 0

/-- The cycle clauses `w v (next p) → w v p`, one for every variable `v < V` and position
`p < N`. Their variables are numbered `k = w v p`. -/
def cycles (V N : ℕ) : Formula :=
  (List.range (V * N)).map fun k => [⟨k, true⟩, ⟨wv V (k % V) (next N (k / V)), false⟩]

/-- The number of literal occurrences of a formula. -/
def size (F : Formula) : ℕ := (F.map List.length).sum

/-- A strict bound on the variable indices of a formula (at least 1). -/
def bound : Formula → ℕ
  | [] => 1
  | C :: F => max (C.foldr (fun l b => max (l.index + 1) b) 1) (bound F)

/-- The splitting step: the chains of all clauses, then the cycle clauses. -/
def split (F : Formula) : Formula :=
  chains (bound F) (size F) 0 F ++ cycles (bound F) (size F)

-- The reduction

/-- The reduction on formulas: split, then pad above every variable in use. -/
def transform (F : Formula) : Formula := pad (bound F * size F + size F) (split F)

/-- The formula a word stands for: the decoded one, or one empty clause if the word encodes
no formula. -/
def parseF (w : Word) : Formula := (decodeCNF w).getD [[]]

/-- The reduction on words. -/
def reduce (w : Word) : Word := encodeCNF (transform (parseF w))

/-- The image is a (3,4) formula. -/
axiom transform_isThreeFour (F : Formula) : IsThreeFour (transform F)

/-- The image is satisfiable exactly when the formula is. -/
axiom transform_sat (F : Formula) : Satisfiable F ↔ Satisfiable (transform F)

/-- The reduction on words is correct. -/
axiom reduce_correct (w : Word) : w ∈ Lax429075.Satisfiability.SAT ↔ reduce w ∈ SAT34

/-- The reduction on words is computable in polynomial time. -/
axiom reduce_polyTime : Nonempty (Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime id id reduce)

end Lax345332.Construction

statements.signature:
reduce_correct : ∀ (w : Lax434930.PolynomialTime.Word),
  Iff (Set.instMembership.mem Lax429075.Satisfiability.SAT w)
    (Set.instMembership.mem Lax345332.ThreeFourSat.SAT34 (Lax345332.Construction.reduce w))

concepts.title: The Reduction from (3,4)-Satisfiability to [2,3]-Bounded 3-SAT
concepts.description:
A (3,4) formula with $C$ clauses has $3C$ literal positions; position $p = 3c + t$ holds the
$t$-th literal of clause $c$. Let $V$ be a strict bound on its variables. The construction
gives every position $p$ its own variable $x_p = v + pV$, where $v$ is the variable at that
position, and produces two kinds of clauses.

* The clauses of three literals are the original clauses, with each literal replaced by the
  copy for its position and keeping its sign.
* The clauses of two literals are the implications $x_{v,p+1} \to x_{v,p}$, that is
  $(x_{v,p} \vee \neg x_{v,p+1})$, for every variable $v < V$ and every position $p$, with
  positions taken cyclically. These chain the copies of $v$ around a cycle, so they all
  take the same value. They are the cycle clauses of the first reduction.

Every literal of the result occurs at most twice. A copy belongs to one position only, so
it appears in at most one clause of three literals, and with one sign. In the cycle of its
variable it is the consequent of one implication and the antecedent of another, which gives
it one positive and one negative occurrence there.

On words, the reduction is the first reduction followed by this construction: a word is
sent to the encoding of a (3,4) formula, that formula is decoded, and the construction is
applied to it and written in the self-delimiting code.

sections.title: Formalization Notes
sections.markdown:
A [2,3]-bounded formula carries its occurrence bound as a field. `build` therefore returns
the formula only when the copies meet the bound (`Occ`) and the empty formula otherwise;
`build_occ` states that the bound is always met, so the second case never arises. The guard
is there because a definition in a concept module may not depend on that module's
statements.

Copies are reduced modulo the number of variables only to give them the type `Fin`; they
are already below it.

`build` is correct only on formulas whose clauses all have three literals (`build_sat`),
which is all that the first reduction produces. On words, correctness is therefore stated
for the composition `reduceB` and not for `toBounded` alone, which reads any word.

import Lax345332.TwoThreeSat
import Lax345332.Construction

/-!
---
title: The Reduction from (3,4)-Satisfiability to [2,3]-Bounded 3-SAT
type: definition
---
A (3,4) formula with $C$ clauses has $3C$ literal positions; position $p = 3c + t$ holds the
$t$-th literal of clause $c$. Let $V$ be a strict bound on its variables. The construction
gives every position $p$ its own variable $x_p = v + pV$, where $v$ is the variable at that
position, and produces two kinds of clauses.

* The clauses of three literals are the original clauses, with each literal replaced by the
  copy for its position and keeping its sign.
* The clauses of two literals are the implications $x_{v,p+1} \to x_{v,p}$, that is
  $(x_{v,p} \vee \neg x_{v,p+1})$, for every variable $v < V$ and every position $p$, with
  positions taken cyclically. These chain the copies of $v$ around a cycle, so they all
  take the same value. They are the cycle clauses of the first reduction.

Every literal of the result occurs at most twice. A copy belongs to one position only, so
it appears in at most one clause of three literals, and with one sign. In the cycle of its
variable it is the consequent of one implication and the antecedent of another, which gives
it one positive and one negative occurrence there.

On words, the reduction is the first reduction followed by this construction: a word is
sent to the encoding of a (3,4) formula, that formula is decoded, and the construction is
applied to it and written in the self-delimiting code.

# Formalization Notes

A [2,3]-bounded formula carries its occurrence bound as a field. `build` therefore returns
the formula only when the copies meet the bound (`Occ`) and the empty formula otherwise;
`build_occ` states that the bound is always met, so the second case never arises. The guard
is there because a definition in a concept module may not depend on that module's
statements.

Copies are reduced modulo the number of variables only to give them the type `Fin`; they
are already below it.

`build` is correct only on formulas whose clauses all have three literals (`build_sat`),
which is all that the first reduction produces. On words, correctness is therefore stated
for the composition `reduceB` and not for `toBounded` alone, which reads any word.
-/

namespace Lax345332.Copies

open Lax429075.CNF Lax345332.Construction Lax345332.TwoThreeSat Lax434930.PolynomialTime

-- Positions and copies

/-- The literal at position `p` of the flattened formula, and a default literal past its
end. -/
def litAt (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) (p : ℕ) : Literal := (F.flatMap id).getD p dflt

/-- The number of literal positions: three per clause. -/
def npos (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : ℕ := 3 * F.length

/-- The number of variables of the result: one copy for every variable and position. -/
def nvars (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : ℕ := bound F * npos F

/-- The copy of the variable at position `p`. -/
def copyVar (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) (p : ℕ) : ℕ := wv (bound F) (litAt F p).index p

/-- The copy that the cycle clause of `kk` mentions negatively: the same variable at the
next position. -/
def succVar (V N kk : ℕ) : ℕ := wv V (kk % V) (next N (kk / V))

/-- The bound on the variables is positive, which the `Fin` indices need. -/
theorem bound_pos (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : 0 < bound F := by
  induction F with
  | nil => exact Nat.one_pos
  | cons C F ih => exact lt_of_lt_of_le ih (le_max_right _ _)

-- The clauses

/-- The literals of the cycle clause `kk`: the copy `kk`, and the negation of its
successor. -/
def twoLit (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) (kk : Fin (nvars F)) (α : Fin 2) :
    Fin (nvars F) × Bool :=
  if α.val = 0 then (kk, true)
  else (⟨succVar (bound F) (npos F) kk.val % nvars F, Nat.mod_lt _ kk.pos⟩, false)

/-- The literals of clause `c`: for `t < 3`, the copy at position `3c + t`, with the sign of
the original literal. -/
def threeLit (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) (c : Fin F.length) (t : Fin 3) :
    Fin (nvars F) × Bool :=
  (⟨copyVar F (3 * c.val + t.val) % nvars F,
      Nat.mod_lt _ (Nat.mul_pos (bound_pos F) (Nat.mul_pos (by decide) c.pos))⟩,
    (litAt F (3 * c.val + t.val)).positive)

/-- The occurrence condition on the construction: every literal occupies at most two
positions. -/
def Occ (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : Prop :=
  ∀ l : Fin (nvars F) × Bool,
    (Finset.univ.filter fun o : (Fin (nvars F) × Fin 2) ⊕ (Fin F.length × Fin 3) =>
      Sum.elim (fun q => twoLit F q.1 q.2) (fun q => threeLit F q.1 q.2) o = l).card ≤ 2

instance (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : Decidable (Occ F) := by unfold Occ; infer_instance

/-- The formula with no variable and no clause. -/
def empty : Lax345332.TwoThreeSat.Formula :=
  ⟨0, 0, 0, fun c => c.elim0, fun c => c.elim0, fun l => l.1.elim0⟩

/-- **The construction.** It has `V·N` variables, where `V` bounds the variables of `F` and
`N = 3C` is its number of positions; the `V·N` cycle clauses; and the `C` clauses of three
literals on the copies. It is the empty formula if the occurrence condition fails. -/
def build (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : Lax345332.TwoThreeSat.Formula :=
  if h : Occ F then ⟨nvars F, nvars F, F.length, twoLit F, threeLit F, h⟩ else empty

-- The reduction

/-- The construction on words: decode a formula, apply `build`, and encode the result. -/
def toBounded (w : Word) : Word := encodeFormula (build (parseF w))

/-- The reduction from satisfiability: the first reduction, then the construction. -/
def reduceB : Word → Word := toBounded ∘ reduce

/-- Every clause of the formula has exactly three literals. -/
def Three (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : Prop := ∀ C ∈ F, C.length = 3

/-- Every literal of the construction occurs at most twice. -/
axiom build_occ (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : Occ F

/-- The result has at most as many variables as literal positions. -/
axiom build_vars_le_slots (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) : (build F).vars ≤ slots (build F)

/-- On a formula whose clauses all have three literals, the construction is satisfiable
exactly when the formula is. -/
axiom build_sat (F : Lax429075.CNF.Formula) (h : Three F) :
    Satisfiable F ↔ (build F).Satisfiable

/-- The reduction from satisfiability is correct on words. -/
axiom reduceB_correct (w : Word) :
    w ∈ Lax429075.Satisfiability.SAT ↔ reduceB w ∈ SAT23

/-- The construction on words is computable in polynomial time. -/
axiom toBounded_polyTime : Nonempty (Turing.TM2ComputableInPolyTime id id toBounded)

end Lax345332.Copies

concepts.sourceText:
import Lax429075.Reductions
import Lax429075.Satisfiability

/-!
---
title: NP-Hardness of (3,4)-SAT
type: theorem
---
*(3,4)-SAT* is satisfiability restricted to formulas in which every clause contains
exactly three literals and every variable occurs at most four times. Tovey proved that it
is NP-hard: every language in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to it.

# Formalization Notes

The restriction is a predicate on the CNF formulas of the archive's Cook–Levin submission,
so the encoding and the notion of satisfiability are shared with unrestricted SAT.
Occurrences are counted with multiplicity.
-/

namespace Lax345332.ThreeFourSat

open Lax429075.CNF Lax434930.PolynomialTime

/-- The number of occurrences of the variable `i` in the formula `F`. -/
def occurrences (F : Formula) (i : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (F.flatMap fun C => C.filter fun l => l.index == i).length

/-- `F` is a *(3,4)* formula: every clause has exactly three literals, and every variable
occurs at most four times. -/
def IsThreeFour (F : Formula) : Prop :=
  (∀ C ∈ F, C.length = 3) ∧ ∀ i, occurrences F i ≤ 4

/-- **(3,4)-SAT** as a language: the encodings of satisfiable (3,4) formulas. -/
def SAT34 : Language :=
  {w | ∃ F : Formula, Lax429075.Encoding.encodeCNF F = w ∧ IsThreeFour F ∧ Satisfiable F}

/-- **Theorem 2.3 (Tovey).** (3,4)-SAT is NP-hard. -/
axiom npHard :
    ∀ A : Language, A ∈ Lax434930.NondeterministicPolynomialTime.NP →
      Lax429075.Reductions.ManyOne A SAT34

end Lax345332.ThreeFourSat

statements.signature:
npHard : ∀ (A : Lax434930.PolynomialTime.Language),
  Set.instMembership.mem Lax434930.NondeterministicPolynomialTime.NP A →
    Lax429075.Reductions.ManyOne A Lax345332.ThreeFourSat.SAT34

concepts.title: NP-Hardness of [2,3]-Bounded 3-SAT
concepts.description:
*[2,3]-bounded 3-SAT* asks whether a formula is satisfiable, where every clause has two or
three literals and every literal, a variable together with a sign, occurs at most twice.
A variable therefore occurs at most twice positively and at most twice negatively, so in at
most four clauses. The problem is NP-hard: every language in NP has a polynomial-time
many-one reduction to it.

Tovey's paper states its theorem for (3,4)-SAT (`ThreeFourSat`). This is the variant that
the scheduling reductions start from, and it follows from the (3,4) case by one more
reduction, given in `Copies`.

sections.title: Formalization Notes
sections.markdown:
The definitions are those of the FairRIS submission, copied so that the two problems are
literally the same: clauses of two literals and clauses of three literals are separate
families, because the constructions that consume such a formula treat them differently.

A formula is written as a binary word in the self-delimiting code of the scheduling
submissions: a number is its binary digits preceded by their count in unary. This is not
the unary code of the Cook–Levin submission that `SAT34` uses, and the theorem is stated
for the words the scheduling submissions read.

The language only contains formulas with at most as many variables as literal positions.
This excludes nothing from a formula in which every variable occurs. It is needed because
the number of variables is written in binary: a word could name exponentially many
variables without using them, and a reduction that writes something for each one could not
run in polynomial time.

The occurrence bound is part of the formula, as a proof that each literal occupies at most
two of the positions inside the clauses.

import Mathlib.Data.List.FinRange

/-!

title: NP-Hardness of [2,3]-Bounded 3-SAT
type: theorem
---

submissions: a number is its binary digits preceded by their count in unary. This is not
the unary code of the Cook–Levin submission that `SAT34` uses, and the theorem is stated
for the words the scheduling submissions read.

The language only contains formulas with at most as many variables as literal positions.
This excludes nothing from a formula in which every variable occurs. It is needed because
the number of variables is written in binary: a word could name exponentially many
variables without using them, and a reduction that writes something for each one could not
run in polynomial time.

The occurrence bound is part of the formula, as a proof that each literal occupies at most
two of the positions inside the clauses.
-/

namespace Lax345332.TwoThreeSat

open Lax434930.PolynomialTime Lax434930.NondeterministicPolynomialTime

/-- A natural number as a binary word: its digits, least significant first, preceded by
their number in unary. -/
def encodeNat (n : ℕ) : Word :=
  List.replicate n.bits.length true ++ [false] ++ n.bits

/-- A **[2,3]-bounded 3-SAT formula** over `vars` variables: `twoClauses` clauses of two
literals and `threeClauses` clauses of three literals, in which every literal — a variable
together with a sign — occupies at most two of the positions of the formula. -/
structure Formula where
  /-- The number of variables. -/
  vars : ℕ
  /-- The number of clauses of two literals. -/
  twoClauses : ℕ
  /-- The number of clauses of three literals. -/
  threeClauses : ℕ
  /-- The literals of the clauses of two literals. -/
  aLit : Fin twoClauses → Fin 2 → Fin vars × Bool
  /-- The literals of the clauses of three literals. -/
  bLit : Fin threeClauses → Fin 3 → Fin vars × Bool
  /-- Every literal occurs at most twice in the formula. -/
  occ_le_two : ∀ l : Fin vars × Bool,
    (Finset.univ.filter fun o : (Fin twoClauses × Fin 2) ⊕ (Fin threeClauses × Fin 3) =>
      Sum.elim (fun q => aLit q.1 q.2) (fun q => bLit q.1 q.2) o = l).card ≤ 2

namespace Formula

variable (φ : Formula)

/-- An assignment of a truth value to every variable. -/
abbrev Assignment := Fin φ.vars → Bool

/-- The assignment `a` satisfies `φ`: every clause, of two or of three literals, contains a
literal that `a` makes true. -/
def Satisfies (a : φ.Assignment) : Prop :=
  (∀ c, ∃ α, a (φ.aLit c α).1 = (φ.aLit c α).2) ∧
  (∀ c, ∃ α, a (φ.bLit c α).1 = (φ.bLit c α).2)

/-- The formula has a satisfying assignment. -/
def Satisfiable : Prop := ∃ a : φ.Assignment, φ.Satisfies a

end Formula

/-- The number of literal positions: two per clause of two literals, three per clause of
three. -/
def slots (φ : Formula) : ℕ := 2 * φ.twoClauses + 3 * φ.threeClauses

/-- A formula as a binary word: the number of variables, the numbers of clauses of two and of
three literals, then the variable and sign of each literal of each clause, the clauses of
two literals first. -/
def encodeFormula (φ : Formula) : Word :=
  encodeNat φ.vars ++ encodeNat φ.twoClauses ++ encodeNat φ.threeClauses ++
    ((List.finRange φ.twoClauses).flatMap fun c =>
      (List.finRange 2).flatMap fun α => encodeNat (φ.aLit c α).1 ++ [(φ.aLit c α).2]) ++
    (List.finRange φ.threeClauses).flatMap fun c =>
      (List.finRange 3).flatMap fun α => encodeNat (φ.bLit c α).1 ++ [(φ.bLit c α).2]

/-- **[2,3]-bounded 3-SAT** as a language: the encodings of satisfiable formulas with at
most as many variables as literal positions. -/
def SAT23 : Language :=
  {w | ∃ φ : Formula, encodeFormula φ = w ∧ φ.vars ≤ slots φ ∧ φ.Satisfiable}

/-- **[2,3]-bounded 3-SAT is NP-hard.** Every language in NP has a polynomial-time
many-one reduction to it. -/
axiom npHard :
    ∀ A : Language, A ∈ NP → Lax429075.Reductions.ManyOne A SAT23

end Lax345332.TwoThreeSat

statements.doc:
**[2,3]-bounded 3-SAT is NP-hard.** Every language in NP has a polynomial-time
many-one reduction to it.

proofs.description: There are as many variables as cycle clauses, each of two positions.

Two positions carrying the same literal lie on the same side, cycle or clause, by the sign
pattern and the injectivity of the copy and successor maps, and there they coincide.

Satisfiability is NP-hard by the Cook–Levin theorem; the reduction to (3,4)-SAT followed
by the copy construction is correct and, as the composition of two polynomial-time
computations, runs in polynomial time; polynomial-time many-one reductions compose.

A word RAM program computes the zeros and ones of the second step: the scan of the first
program decodes the (3,4) formula into arrays, and the header, the cycle clauses and the
copied clauses are written in the self-delimiting binary code, within a fourth-degree
polynomial number of instructions. Polynomial time on the word RAM transfers to a Turing
machine.

The first step is correct and its image is a formula of three-literal clauses, on which
the copy construction preserves and reflects satisfiability; the encoding is injective, so
a word in the language is the encoding of the formula built.

Forwards, every copy takes the value of its variable; backwards, the cycle clauses force
the copies of a variable to agree, and the common value satisfies the original clause.

The reduction is a word RAM program on the zeros and ones of its input: a finite-state
scan decodes the formula into arrays of literal indices, signs and clause numbers; one
pass tabulates where each clause ends; the chain clauses are then written clause by
clause and the cycle clauses position by position, each with its padding and its three
gadgets, in the encoding's unary code. Polynomial time on the word RAM transfers to a
Turing machine.

Satisfiability is NP-hard by the Cook–Levin theorem, the reduction is correct and runs in
polynomial time, and polynomial-time many-one reductions compose.

The encoding is injective and a decoded word is the encoding of what it decodes to, so the
statement is that of the reduction on formulas; a word that encodes nothing is sent to the
image of an unsatisfiable formula.

Padding makes every clause three literals long. Below the padding base the occurrence counts
are those of the split formula, at most three; above it a variable belongs to one gadget of
one clause, where it occurs at most four times, the forced variable three times in the
gadget and once as padding.

Splitting: an assignment of `F` is copied to every position and the link after a literal is
set to "no literal so far is true"; conversely the cycle makes all copies of a variable
equal, and a chain with all literals false propagates a true link into its last clause.
Padding: the gadgets force the padding literals false, and can always be satisfied.
